作者：Peter Yang 账号：@petergyang 简介：Practical AI tutorials and interviews for busy people | Get my best AI skills and guides at https://t.co/6VAA6p81x6
Think about how much time we all waste waiting on hold or trying to navigate legacy phone systems ("say 1 to proceed" 🤮).
That's why I love Grok @Bot's new phone call feature. Try it with these 5 use cases:
1. Negotiate any bill
"Call Comcast about my internet bill. I pay $84 a month and a competitor offers $49. Ask for a lower price."
2. Cancel subscriptions
"Call my gym and cancel my membership. Here's my account info. Turn down any retention offers and get a confirmation number."
3. Wait on hold
"Call the airline about my canceled flight. Here's my confirmation code. Stay on hold until you reach a person, then ask for a full refund."
4. Make reservations
"Call this restaurant and book a table for 4 on Friday at 7pm. If that's taken, anything between 6 and 8 works."
5. Get contractor quotes
"Call these 3 contractors about replacing my water heater. Ask each one for price and earliest start date. Then put the answers in a table."
Note that this only works with US numbers for now but it's nevertheless a game changer.
📌 Watch my new video to see how it works with a real call: https://t.co/UWt3SanRSN

My two favorite default skills on Claude Code, still, that seem relatively less used are a) /insights and b) /playground..
For insights, I have a regular cron job that runs this now every two weeks. It tells me all the best ways to upgrade my setup. I pair it with X bookmarks that show all the new ways to build a software factory. It's a self improving loop on how I use Claude Code + what the industry thinks I should move to.
For playground, it's the best way to visualize what's happening in the workflow. I ask it to show me architecture of esoteric Github's to simulating a full learning loop on my side project. My new favorite thing is to pair Codex + Claude Code on this skill and ask it to find dead code, hot pathways, latency improvements.

item.description:
作者：Guillermo Rauch 账号：@rauchg 简介：@vercel CEO
I've been looking forward to this day, because Vercel has an internal security agent that is **astonishingly effective** (lovingly called @𝚑𝚊𝚌𝚔𝚎𝚛). Every single line of code gets audited, automatically.
You can now get the same power. Just enable it on all your repos (this product works whether you host on Vercel or not) and your peace of mind will increase tremendously. You'll see it catch things that every other agent misses.
Why: you cannot just bank on your engineers having a skill installed, prompting "please make secure", or rolling the weights' dice that the code is good out of the gate.
The other cool thing about this is that this was entirely developed by our security team. A lot of companies out there are probably in a mad rush right now trying to staff up. If you wanted to 'download a security team' as software, this is the closest you get today.

item.title: Friday was my last day at Anthropic. Two years ago, when Claude Code was a small internal tool, I asked it to build an RL env. I steered it for tens of hours but never manually wrote a line of code. It worked, I was hooked, and I joined the team. When we first launched, most people approved every ...
item.description:
作者：Cat Wu 账号：@_catwu 简介：claude code + cowork @anthropicai, prev: @dagster, @scale_ai
Friday was my last day at Anthropic.
Two years ago, when Claude Code was a small internal tool, I asked it to build an RL env. I steered it for tens of hours but never manually wrote a line of code. It worked, I was hooked, and I joined the team.
When we first launched, most people approved every permission prompt by hand and mostly used Claude to answer questions and write tests.
Today, the default is trusting Claude's judgment to auto-approve. Claude does large migrations and builds new products.
Helping build Claude Code into an industry-defining product has been the journey of a lifetime.
Thank you to the incredible team behind Claude Code, Cowork, and Tag. These products are the sum of thousands of great ideas from you. I'll miss working with you all.
Thank you to our users for embracing a new way of working. Your constant feedback shaped so much of what we shipped and your stories made the work so meaningful.
Excited to see what you all make next!

item.title: The divergence in AI output weirdly may be the highest it’s ever been, even though adoption is the broadest it’s ever been. A few years ago the best productivity gains you could get, even in the most capability-aligned field (like coding), was maybe 30-50% better productivity if you were very good...
item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
The divergence in AI output weirdly may be the highest it’s ever been, even though adoption is the broadest it’s ever been.
A few years ago the best productivity gains you could get, even in the most capability-aligned field (like coding), was maybe 30-50% better productivity if you were very good at it. You’d spend a decent chunk of time cleaning up the mistakes of models, the context windows were too limited to do any long running work, and the interfaces required highly synchronous interactions.
Now, the models can do far longer tasks at a time with limited human interaction. The harnesses support agentic work that can take on these larger tasks. The models are trained on vastly better datasets for a growing array of domains so you have to intervene far less. And we have systems that better support working with many agents at once.
In just a two year timespan, the upper limits on productivity gains have gone from 30-50% to now likely 5-10X depending on the field. So we’ve gone from an environment where living at the frontier vs. not paying attention at all could be an order of magnitude difference in your output.
This distance is only getting wider from here given the rate of progress we’re likely to see with RSI. Crazy times.

item.title: Ep 96: Nebius CTO on Racing the Hyperscalers Before AWS Wakes Up
item.description:
播客：Unsupervised Learning
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:15 If NVIDIA could have bought... Like, could have produced, like, 10 x the chips, this whole market would have been shaped differently. Yeah. Because there is not enough capacity for their scale, this is a relatively small business for them. For the hyperscalers, it's not just a matter of, like, sales.
Speaker 1 | 00:15 - 00:29 It's also a matter of changing the infrastructure that was built at scale for other kinds of workloads. This is a massive investment on their part that needs to be justified by the size of a potential business, and it's not that there yet.
Speaker 2 | 00:33 - 01:08 The emergence of Nebius and the other hyperscaler competitors these past years has been a fascinating part of the AI story. It's something I've really been interested in, and so it was a lot of fun to have Nebius' CTO, Neela, on the podcast because we're able to dig into a bunch of interesting things about the business and how the space has unfolded. We talked about Nebius' really interesting origin story and the original relationship with Yandex and how the company came to be. We talked about what it's like to be inside one of these companies, how Nebius works, you know, with NVIDIA, what it looks like to get their next generation of chips live. We talked about why the opportunity actually existed and why AWS, GCP, Azure, didn't just capture this entire market.
Speaker 2 | 01:09 - 01:30 We also talked about Danila's view on a bunch of new technologies like Disag, Inference, among other things. All in all, just awesome to get to talk with someone who's at the epicenter of the AI infrastructure market about his thoughts on everything about where the space is headed. I think folks will really enjoy it. Without further ado, here he is. I guess I'd love to talk just maybe about the broader, like, AI cloud market, you know, today.
Speaker 2 | 01:30 - 01:48 And I think that there's a few maybe larger and prominent public, you know, I guess, neo clouds. And then, you know, it feels like there's a new one getting funded every day. I know you don't like that term. But maybe just talk a little bit about how you think about what differentiates... Like, some of our listeners are probably thinking like, you know, all that really matters is just access to GPUs and like, you know, you...
Speaker 2 | 01:48 - 01:54 Wherever you can get them, you go. Maybe maybe use that as a straw man and and tell us why that's not the case.
Speaker 1 | 01:54 - 02:27 Well, I'm obviously biased. Because like, first of all, I'm a software person. And our product and business was launched on the idea that software is the moat. Right? So your ability to serve the customers that consume, I don't know, tens of thousands GPUs, of GPUs, and then one interconnected cluster with the same platform as you serve, like a self-service customer that runs one GPU for half an hour, was our value prop from the very beginning.
Speaker 1 | 02:27 - 02:52 So we believe that this is extremely important. Being able to build large scale, but have the possibility almost like sell it in retail in a sense. This is what we think like definitely differentiates us from the market, from everyone on the market. Like a small remark, Neo Clouds. Hate that term, like with a passion.
Speaker 1 | 02:52 - 03:16 Because like, it started as a distinction, as in these are kind of cloud companies that are doing this weird, strange new thing. But then everyone wants it in that market. So like, when we started, there were like, I don't know, five, seven companies that were in this area that were called NeoClouds. Now I think it's closer to, like, three to 500.
Speaker 2 | 03:16 - 03:16 Yeah.
Speaker 1 | 03:16 - 03:31 Depending on what you even are ready to call a Neo Cloud to the scale. And we we really don't like this stretched umbrella term anymore. We are the AI Cloud. We don't care. Like, let others...
Speaker 1 | 03:31 - 03:48 Other guys beat Neo Clouds. We are the AI Cloud, And this is our mental model. We are not competing with the Neo Cloud markets. We kind of believe we are past that. Our next competition point is taking on AWS and Google Cloud.
Speaker 1 | 03:49 - 04:10 Yes, we are way smaller. Yes, our revenue is like, what, I think 1% of AWS nowadays. But we are running fast. We serve a very particular market. We have a bet that this is the market that is going to grow, that is going to explode.
Speaker 1 | 04:10 - 04:42 So people are concerned that these investments are huge. People put a lot into the infrastructure, etcetera, etcetera. My view, if I compare what we see in the market with what was there two years ago, we are barely scratching the surface. I think the overall demand in the next three years will increase tenfold, hundredfold maybe. So we are at the verge of another explosive growth.
Speaker 1 | 04:42 - 04:56 Right now, we see these huge facilities. But a lot of those are privately owned for internal needs of certain companies. Right? So they're like, Elon Musk is talking about his Colossus cluster. And it's like, it's a man's scale.
Speaker 1 | 04:56 - 05:07 Like, really, it's like real solid, large scale thing. But it's not for the broader market. Right? It's for their internal needs. Maybe for some partners that they do something.
Speaker 2 | 05:07 - 05:08 For Anthropic if...
Speaker 1 | 05:09 - 05:27 Yeah. Anthropic and OpenAI are messing the, like, the capacity, but they do it for their own product. And this is like a wholly separate discussion. These companies will essentially want to be everything. They will want to be the internet and contain everything and every product and every capacity angle within themselves.
Speaker 1 | 05:29 - 06:00 There is a question of Google, Meta, and Microsoft who have a lot of capacity but are constantly juggling and struggling between, like, giving it out to the market for... Like, to rent or giving it out to internal teams. Because all of all of these companies are extremely, like, machine learning AI enabled. They need a ton of capacity for internal usage, for runtime and for research. So they have to constantly juggle this.
Speaker 1 | 06:00 - 06:15 So our bet is that there is a niche for an independent, as in not affiliated with a large company with huge internal consumption player that will serve the markets of the mid tier players who want to be the large companies.
Speaker 2 | 06:16 - 06:28 I thought it'd be interesting for our listeners to talk a little bit about the history of Nebius. I feel like it's a really interesting path that you've you've... And, you know, had to end up here. And so maybe just talk a little bit about how the business came to be.
Speaker 1 | 06:28 - 06:47 I will start with the, like, with the moment I've joined. Right? So I am CTO of the company, but I've been with the company from the very beginning, like, since before it was called Nibius. So the new company is established, I think, during 2024 also. The deal was finalized.
Speaker 1 | 06:47 - 06:57 We finally announced our separation from Yandex. No connections to the Russian assets anymore, clean slate, etcetera, etcetera, etcetera. And that was it.
Speaker 2 | 06:57 - 07:26 You know, people have come to these AI cloud businesses in different ways. And, obviously, you know, I felt like the Yandex team was, like, legendarily really, really strong, you know, on on the engineering side. You know, a lot of folks building AI clouds came from, like, crypto or energy or, like, not not necessarily the same, you know, maybe technical heritage. To what extent, I guess, was the Yandex experience really relevant? And to what extent was it like, you know, it turns out no one knows how to build a GPU cloud because it's all kinda new and, you know, there's there's...
Speaker 2 | 07:26 - 07:27 Everyone's learning on the fly.
Speaker 1 | 07:27 - 08:04 First, we had and still have the core team that supports the hardware side of business that came from Yandex t...
